query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: If a powder-metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy is subjected to a short dwell at roughly 800–900 °C in a controlled oxidizing environment to form a stable oxide-based barrier layer, then its resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion (tribo-corrosion) at elevated temperatures should be significantly higher than that of conventional structural alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated, powder-metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy
generation.intervention: Engineered oxide-based surface treatment via short dwell (e.g., several minutes) at approximately 800–900 °C in a tailored environment to promote stable spinel-type oxide formation
generation.conditions: Exposed to simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive media at elevated temperatures typical of extreme service environments
generation.structural_mediator: In-situ formed oxide/spinel surface layer on AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5
generation.mechanism: The durable oxide-based barrier layer reduces both mechanical damage via wear and chemical attack via corrosion by limiting interfacial reactions under tribo-corrosive conditions
generation.predicted_outcome: A significantly lower tribo-corrosion rate compared to conventional alloys exposed to the same conditions, potentially on the order of multiple times lower material loss
generation.baseline: Conventional high-temperature structural alloys lacking protective spinel layers experience accelerated oxidation and wear under similar tribo-corrosion conditions
generation.boundary: Performance demonstrated for moderate to high temperatures (up to around 900 °C); behavior remains unverified for more aggressive chemical media or higher temperatures
generation.uncertainty: Direct tribo-corrosion testing data on oxide-engineered AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 are limited; long-term stability of spinel layers under continuously changing environments is not fully established

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct comparative tribo-corrosion tests on oxide-treated AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 coupons and untreated or conventional alloy coupons (e.g., Ni-based superalloys) in a temperature range from 400 °C to 900 °C within a reactive environment (e.g., controlled humidity or molten salt spray). Apply reciprocating or rotating wear contact while immersing specimens in the corrosive medium at a fixed load to induce tribo-corrosion.
measurements: Mass loss or volumetric wear rate
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxide-treated AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 experiences comparable or higher combined wear and corrosion rates than conventional alloys under the same test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6

decision.trend: Powder-metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloys were explored for high-temperature wear applications. By performing reciprocating wear tests from room temperature up to 900 °C, researchers noted that wear resistance and friction behavior improved at higher temperatures due to the in-situ formation of protective oxide/spinel layers. These layers reduced wear and friction but were tested primarily under dry sliding conditions rather than a combined corrosive and wear environment, leaving tribo-corrosion performance less well characterized.
decision.unsolved: Although the formation of protective oxide/spinel phases enhances wear performance at elevated temperatures, the material’s resistance specifically under tribo-corrosion conditions (synergistic mechanical wear and chemical attack) remains insufficiently examined. The stability and protective nature of these oxides in a corrosive medium at high temperature need further validation.
decision.lever: Engineered oxide-based barrier layers formed in controlled atmospheres (e.g., short dwell at ≈800–900 °C in a tailored environment) to create a robust tribo-corrosion resistant surface finish
decision.why: Building on the observed benefits of in-situ spinel formation at high temperature, deliberately establishing a stable oxide layer at or near the surface can enhance both wear and corrosion protection simultaneously in severe tribo-corrosion environments.
